Severity classification Classify every finding before writing outputs: - **BLOCKING** — merge would cause a bug, security issue, data loss, or CI break. Must be fixed. - **IMPORTANT** — real maintainability or correctness issue. Strongly prefer fixing before merge. - **SUGGESTION** — optional improvement, style, or future polish. Does not block merge. When in doubt, start one level higher; downgrade only after confirming the risk is negligible. ## 7. Exhaustive single-pass review Treat **every** review as the final and only review pass. The author will not get another chance to catch missed findings cheaply. - Do not defer SUGGESTION or IMPORTANT items to a later round because a BLOCKING issue exists. - After classifying all findings, re-read every changed file and ask: *"What else is improvable here?"* - Before writing outputs, verify that no obvious quality, maintainability, or correctness issue was left unreported. - Aim to surface the maximum number of actionable findings in this single iteration. ## 8. If `pr_diff.txt` is truncated, run `git diff origin/{baseBranch}...HEAD` to locate the correct line numbers. BLOCKING / IMPORTANT / SUGGESTION"] SEVERITY --> EXHAUST["7. Exhaustive pass:
re-read changed files,
surface ALL remaining issues"] EXHAUST --> OUTPUT["8. Write outputs:
pr_review.json · pr_review_general.md · pr_review_comments/*.md"] OUTPUT --> END([End]) ``` ## 1. Input context — MANDATORY reading order ```mermaid flowchart TD subgraph PR_CONTEXT["⚠️ PR-specific files (read first)"] P1["1️⃣ instruction.md (repo root) — project stack, conventions"] P2["2️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_info.md — PR title, author, branch, description"] P3["3️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_diff.txt — the diff to review"] P4["4️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_files.txt — list of changed files"] P5["5️⃣ input/TICKET/ci_failures.md — CI failures = BLOCKING (last 500 lines)"] P5_FULL["5️⃣ input/TICKET/ci_failures_full.log — full CI logs"] P6["6️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_discussions.md + pr_discussions_raw.json — existing comments"] P1 --> P2 --> P3 --> P4 --> P5 --> P5_FULL --> P6 end subgraph TICKET_CONTEXT["Ticket context (for understanding PR purpose)"] T1["7️⃣ input/TICKET/ticket.md — linked ticket description, ACs"] T2["8️⃣ input/TICKET/comments.md — ticket discussion if present"] T3["9️⃣ input/TICKET/parent-*.md — parent story context"] T4["🔟 input/TICKET/confluence/*.md — linked specifications"] T1 --> T2 --> T3 --> T4 end subgraph RULE["⚠️ Rule"] R1["If file exists in input/ → read locally, do NOT re-fetch via dmtools"] end PR_CONTEXT --> TICKET_CONTEXT --> RULE ``` Read PR files to understand WHAT changed. Read ticket files to understand WHY it changed and verify against requirements. ## 2. Diff checklist — apply to `pr_diff.txt` For every hunk, ask at least these questions: - [ ] Does the change match the ticket scope? Any scope creep? - [ ] Are new or changed public APIs contract-safe for existing callers? - [ ] Is user/external input validated, sanitized, or escaped? - [ ] Are secrets, tokens, or PATs handled safely — not logged, not interpolated into shell scripts? - [ ] Are new or modified files present under `testing/` in a non-test-automation PR? - [ ] Is dead code, unused imports, or obvious duplication introduced? - [ ] Are error paths handled, or are failures silently swallowed? - [ ] Are new dependencies justified and compatible with the existing stack? - [ ] Beyond blockers: what other maintainability, correctness, or quality improvements are visible in the changed code? ## 3. Changed-file deep read Do not review from the diff alone. Read the full content of every changed file: - imports and dependencies - class/method responsibilities and adherence to SRP / OOP principles - naming consistency with the rest of the codebase - error handling, logging, and edge cases - test coverage for changed behavior - backward-compatibility and migration impact ## 4. Impact analysis (CodeGraph or grep fallback) Use CodeGraph to find "what could break": - `codegraph_callers` / `codegraph_callees` on modified public symbols - `codegraph_search` for: `PAT_TOKEN`, `secrets.`, `github.token`, `previousViewModel` - `codegraph_impact` before flagging architectural changes **If CodeGraph unavailable**, use grep and document it: ```bash grep -rn "changedFunctionName" --include="*.ts" . grep -rn "secrets\.\|github\.token" . ``` ## 5. Severity classification Classify every finding before writing outputs: - **BLOCKING** — merge would cause a bug, security issue, data loss, or CI break. Must be fixed. - **IMPORTANT** — real maintainability or correctness issue. Strongly prefer fixing before merge. - **SUGGESTION** — optional improvement, style, or future polish. Does not block merge. When in doubt, start one level higher; downgrade only after confirming the risk is negligible. ## 7. Exhaustive single-pass review Treat **every** review as the final and only review pass. The author will not get another chance to catch missed findings cheaply. - Do not defer SUGGESTION or IMPORTANT items to a later round because a BLOCKING issue exists. - After classifying all findings, re-read every changed file and ask: *"What else is improvable here?"* - Before writing outputs, verify that no obvious quality, maintainability, or correctness issue was left unreported. - Aim to surface the maximum number of actionable findings in this single iteration. ## 8. Outputs Write the standard review artifacts: - `outputs/pr_review.json` — structured data with `recommendation`, `summary`, `inlineComments`, `issueCounts` - `outputs/pr_review_general.md` — 1-2 paragraph general PR comment - `outputs/pr_review_comments/*.md` — one file per detailed inline comment **Inline comment lines must be present in the PR diff.** GitHub review threads can only be attached to added or context lines inside a diff hunk. If `pr_diff.txt` is truncated, run `git diff origin/{baseBranch}...HEAD` to locate the correct line numbers. Now let me think about remaining deeper review aspects:

**A. Correctness of the new single-flight guard — one more edge case:**

```dart
Future<void> _persist() {
  final inFlight = _persistPass;
  if (inFlight != null) {
    _persistDirty = true;
    return inFlight;
  }
  return _persistPass = _persistLoop();
}
```

`_persistLoop` sets `_persistPass = null` in its `finally`. Consider: loop A running. Trigger B joins (dirty=true, awaits A). Loop A's current sweep finishes, dirty→true so re-sweeps. During re-sweep, trigger C joins (dirty=true, awaits A). Loop A re-sweeps again... converges when no more triggers land during sweeps. Fine.

Now the subtle one: **`_persistSoon` fire-and-forget with `.catchError` on a JOINED future.** `inFlight.catchError(...)` attaches to loop A's future. If loop A fails, both B's catchError and (for the finalizer) the try/catch handle it. But there's an asymmetry: when `_persistSoon` STARTS the loop (B is the starter), the loop future is wrapped: `unawaited(_persist().catchError(...))`. The un-wrapped loop future has ONE handler (the catchError's derived future is unawaited — but the ORIGINAL future's error flows into `.catchError`, which returns a NEW future whose error is swallowed... wait, does the original future count as "handled"? `.catchError` registers a handler on the original future — yes, handled.

When the finalizer STARTS the loop: `await _persist()` inside try/catch. Handled.

But here's an edge: the finalizer STARTS the loop and awaits it in try/catch; MEANWHILE a `_persistSoon` joins with `.catchError`. The loop SUCCEEDS. Fine.

Another edge: `_persistSoon` joins, attaching `.catchError`; the finalizer ALSO joined earlier via `await` in try/catch. Both handle. Fine.

What if `_persistSoon` starts the loop and its `catchError` swallows; then dispose() happens mid-loop? Loop continues, appends to session — session file ops on disposed service. `dispose` doesn't null `_session`. Pre-existing semantics (old code same). Not a regression.

**B. The dirty-flag re-run: `_persistedCount` last-writer-wins claim.**

`_persistUnchecked` sets `_persistedCount = all.length` at the end. Concurrent mutation of `_agent.state.messages` DURING the sweep: `for (final message in all.skip(_persistedCount))` — `all` is the LIVE list (`_agent.state.messages`). If a message is appended to the list WHILE the for-loop iterates it, the iterator sees it (live list) — that's fine, and `_persistedCount = all.length` at the end covers it. But could a message be REMOVED mid-sweep (reset/branch-switch)? `_persistedCount` bookkeeping vs. concurrent `reset()` — pre-existing hazard, unchanged by this PR.

Hmm — one NEW subtle issue though: the old chain guaranteed strict ordering: `_persistChain = _persistChain.then((_) => _persist())`. Each queued pass started only after the previous completed. The new single-flight loop merges passes but sweeps the same live state — equivalent or better. 

**C. `await inFlight` returns the LOOP's completion — including ALL coalesced re-sweeps.** The finalizer's comment claims "Awaiting this returns only when every pass queued so far has drained". TRUE: a trigger landing before the loop's final dirty-check causes another sweep; the await covers it.

BUT WAIT — one real gap: a trigger landing AFTER `_persistPass = null` (loop ended) starts a NEW loop. If the finalizer's `await _persist()` had joined the OLD loop, and a NEW pass starts after the old loop ended but before the finalizer's compaction... that's inherent to any concurrent system — the finalizer awaited only what was queued when IT called `_persist()`. Fine.

**D. Zone comment rationale** — "a chain head created at construction captures that zone" — `_persistChain = Future<void>.value()` was a field initializer, capturing the construction zone; chained `.then` listeners run in the head's zone. Under `tester.runAsync` (which runs in a different zone in fake_async widget tests), timers scheduled by the head zone never fire inside runAsync... plausible rationale for widget tests. The new approach stores `null` when idle, and `_persistLoop()`'s future is created in the CALLER's zone. OK — the comment is justified, and tests pass.

**E. Missing test for the coalescing path itself?** The new tests verify end state. There's no direct unit test asserting `_persistDirty` coalescing (that a trigger landing mid-sweep produces exactly ONE extra sweep). The second test's name says "coalesced persist passes land the full final state by idle" — it indirectly exercises the join path (finalizer joins in-flight pass from `_onMessageEnd`'s `_persistSoon`). Given the private fields, an additional test would need @visibleForTesting seams — not worth blocking. The end-state assertions are the right level.

**F. Test uses `(await repo.list()).single`** — if the session wasn't materialized, `.single` would throw StateError — acceptable in a test (fail = fail). Fine.

**G. `_DeferredAppendEnv implements ExecutionEnv`** — brittle to interface growth, but compile-time safe (implements forces updates). Alternative: `extends MemoryExecutionEnv` + override `appendFile` would be much shorter and auto-inherit new members. Is `MemoryExecutionEnv` a class with non-trivial constructor? Let me check — if it can be extended, the delegation boilerplate (~80 lines) could be avoided. Let me check MemoryExecutionEnv's declaration.

Actually wait — `MemoryExecutionEnv` is from `package:fa/sandbox/memory_shell.dart`. Let me check whether it's designed for extension (fields needing constructor args, private members). If extendable, the test helper could be `class _DeferredAppendEnv extends MemoryExecutionEnv { @override Future<...> appendFile(...) async { await Future.delayed(Duration.zero); return super.appendFile(path, content); }` — dramatically less boilerplate and immune to interface additions. blocks.text:
The ci.yml perf gate selects `flutter_app/lib/services/agent_service(_sessions)?\.dart` changes — the perf gate (`--tags perf`) will run for this PR since `agent_service.dart` changed. That's a CI concern (the perf-tagged leg will run), not something I need to validate locally.

Also — let me check the CRAP gate for flutter_app (line 1192: `crap4dart analyze`), plus check whether flutter_app has a crap4dart threshold that the new `_persistLoop` complexity could trip. Probably fine — the function is tiny.

Now let me think about remaining deeper review aspects:

**A. Correctness of the new single-flight guard — one more edge case:**

```dart
Future<void> _persist() {
  final inFlight = _persistPass;
  if (inFlight != null) {
    _persistDirty = true;
    return inFlight;
  }
  return _persistPass = _persistLoop();
}
```

`_persistLoop` sets `_persistPass = null` in its `finally`. Consider: loop A running. Trigger B joins (dirty=true, awaits A). Loop A's current sweep finishes, dirty→true so re-sweeps. During re-sweep, trigger C joins (dirty=true, awaits A). Loop A re-sweeps again... converges when no more triggers land during sweeps. Fine.

Now the subtle one: **`_persistSoon` fire-and-forget with `.catchError` on a JOINED future.** `inFlight.catchError(...)` attaches to loop A's future. If loop A fails, both B's catchError and (for the finalizer) the try/catch handle it. But there's an asymmetry: when `_persistSoon` STARTS the loop (B is the starter), the loop future is wrapped: `unawaited(_persist().catchError(...))`. The un-wrapped loop future has ONE handler (the catchError's derived future is unawaited — but the ORIGINAL future's error flows into `.catchError`, which returns a NEW future whose error is swallowed... wait, does the original future count as "handled"? `.catchError` registers a handler on the original future — yes, handled.

When the finalizer STARTS the loop: `await _persist()` inside try/catch. Handled.

But here's an edge: the finalizer STARTS the loop and awaits it in try/catch; MEANWHILE a `_persistSoon` joins with `.catchError`. The loop SUCCEEDS. Fine.

Another edge: `_persistSoon` joins, attaching `.catchError`; the finalizer ALSO joined earlier via `await` in try/catch. Both handle. Fine.

What if `_persistSoon` starts the loop and its `catchError` swallows; then dispose() happens mid-loop? Loop continues, appends to session — session file ops on disposed service. `dispose` doesn't null `_session`. Pre-existing semantics (old code same). Not a regression.

**B. The dirty-flag re-run: `_persistedCount` last-writer-wins claim.**

`_persistUnchecked` sets `_persistedCount = all.length` at the end. Concurrent mutation of `_agent.state.messages` DURING the sweep: `for (final message in all.skip(_persistedCount))` — `all` is the LIVE list (`_agent.state.messages`). If a message is appended to the list WHILE the for-loop iterates it, the iterator sees it (live list) — that's fine, and `_persistedCount = all.length` at the end covers it. But could a message be REMOVED mid-sweep (reset/branch-switch)? `_persistedCount` bookkeeping vs. concurrent `reset()` — pre-existing hazard, unchanged by this PR.

Hmm — one NEW subtle issue though: the old chain guaranteed strict ordering: `_persistChain = _persistChain.then((_) => _persist())`. Each queued pass started only after the previous completed. The new single-flight loop merges passes but sweeps the same live state — equivalent or better. 

**C. `await inFlight` returns the LOOP's completion — including ALL coalesced re-sweeps.** The finalizer's comment claims "Awaiting this returns only when every pass queued so far has drained". TRUE: a trigger landing before the loop's final dirty-check causes another sweep; the await covers it.

BUT WAIT — one real gap: a trigger landing AFTER `_persistPass = null` (loop ended) starts a NEW loop. If the finalizer's `await _persist()` had joined the OLD loop, and a NEW pass starts after the old loop ended but before the finalizer's compaction... that's inherent to any concurrent system — the finalizer awaited only what was queued when IT called `_persist()`. Fine.

**D. Zone comment rationale** — "a chain head created at construction captures that zone" — `_persistChain = Future<void>.value()` was a field initializer, capturing the construction zone; chained `.then` listeners run in the head's zone. Under `tester.runAsync` (which runs in a different zone in fake_async widget tests), timers scheduled by the head zone never fire inside runAsync... plausible rationale for widget tests. The new approach stores `null` when idle, and `_persistLoop()`'s future is created in the CALLER's zone. OK — the comment is justified, and tests pass.

**E. Missing test for the coalescing path itself?** The new tests verify end state. There's no direct unit test asserting `_persistDirty` coalescing (that a trigger landing mid-sweep produces exactly ONE extra sweep). The second test's name says "coalesced persist passes land the full final state by idle" — it indirectly exercises the join path (finalizer joins in-flight pass from `_onMessageEnd`'s `_persistSoon`). Given the private fields, an additional test would need @visibleForTesting seams — not worth blocking. The end-state assertions are the right level.

**F. Test uses `(await repo.list()).single`** — if the session wasn't materialized, `.single` would throw StateError — acceptable in a test (fail = fail). Fine.

**G. `_DeferredAppendEnv implements ExecutionEnv`** — brittle to interface growth, but compile-time safe (implements forces updates). Alternative: `extends MemoryExecutionEnv` + override `appendFile` would be much shorter and auto-inherit new members. Is `MemoryExecutionEnv` a class with non-trivial constructor? Let me check — if it can be extended, the delegation boilerplate (~80 lines) could be avoided. Let me check MemoryExecutionEnv's declaration.

Actually wait — `MemoryExecutionEnv` is from `package:fa/sandbox/memory_shell.dart`. Let me check whether it's designed for extension (fields needing constructor args, private members). If extendable, the test helper could be `class _DeferredAppendEnv extends MemoryExecutionEnv { @override Future<...> appendFile(...) async { await Future.delayed(Duration.zero); return super.appendFile(path, content); }` — dramatically less boilerplate and immune to interface additions. Let me check if other tests in the repo delegate like this (pattern consistency) or extend.

blocks.text:
Senior Code Reviewer & Security Expert You are an agent triggered to perform a specific task. All required context — ticket description, PR diff, CI status, and related materials — has already been prepared in the `input/` folder. Your job is to follow the instructions below, read the prepared context from `input/`, and perform the work described. Do not ask for identifiers; the context is already available locally. ```mermaid flowchart TD G1["⚠️ Review Guidelines — evaluate against existing codebase patterns"] G2["Before reviewing, explore the project's code structure, architecture, and testing patterns"] G3["If AGENTS.md exists → READ it — defines coding styles to check against"] G4["Flag deviations from established patterns unless justified in PR description"] G1 --> G2 --> G3 --> G4 ``` # PR Review General Guidelines ## Review flow ```mermaid flowchart TD START([PR ready for review]) --> READ["1. Read input context:
instruction.md, ticket.md, pr_info.md,
pr_diff.txt, pr_files.txt, ci_failures.md,
ci_failures_full.log, pr_discussions.md,
pr_discussions_raw.json"] READ --> DIFF["2. Run diff checklist on pr_diff.txt"] DIFF --> FILES["3. Read full content of every changed file"] FILES --> CODEGRAPH["4. Use CodeGraph:
callers/callees of changed symbols,
search for sensitive patterns,
impact analysis"] CODEGRAPH --> DIMS["5. Evaluate review dimensions:
Security · Architecture/OOP · Code quality
Test coverage · Duplication · Backward compatibility"] DIMS --> SEVERITY["6. Classify each finding:
BLOCKING / IMPORTANT / SUGGESTION"] SEVERITY --> EXHAUST["7. Exhaustive pass:
re-read changed files,
surface ALL remaining issues"] EXHAUST --> OUTPUT["8. Write outputs:
pr_review.json · pr_review_general.md · pr_review_comments/*.md"] OUTPUT --> END([End]) ``` ## 1. Input context — MANDATORY reading order ```mermaid flowchart TD subgraph PR_CONTEXT["⚠️ PR-specific files (read first)"] P1["1️⃣ instruction.md (repo root) — project stack, conventions"] P2["2️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_info.md — PR title, author, branch, description"] P3["3️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_diff.txt — the diff to review"] P4["4️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_files.txt — list of changed files"] P5["5️⃣ input/TICKET/ci_failures.md — CI failures = BLOCKING (last 500 lines)"] P5_FULL["5️⃣ input/TICKET/ci_failures_full.log — full CI logs"] P6["6️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_discussions.md + pr_discussions_raw.json — existing comments"] P1 --> P2 --> P3 --> P4 --> P5 --> P5_FULL --> P6 end subgraph TICKET_CONTEXT["Ticket context (for understanding PR purpose)"] T1["7️⃣ input/TICKET/ticket.md — linked ticket description, ACs"] T2["8️⃣ input/TICKET/comments.md — ticket discussion if present"] T3["9️⃣ input/TICKET/parent-*.md — parent story context"] T4["🔟 input/TICKET/confluence/*.md — linked specifications"] T1 --> T2 --> T3 --> T4 end subgraph RULE["⚠️ Rule"] R1["If file exists in input/ → read locally, do NOT re-fetch via dmtools"] end PR_CONTEXT --> TICKET_CONTEXT --> RULE ``` Read PR files to understand WHAT changed. Read ticket files to understand WHY it changed and verify against requirements. ## 2. Diff checklist — apply to `pr_diff.txt` For every hunk, ask at least these questions: - [ ] Does the change match the ticket scope? Any scope creep? - [ ] Are new or changed public APIs contract-safe for existing callers? - [ ] Is user/external input validated, sanitized, or escaped? - [ ] Are secrets, tokens, or PATs handled safely — not logged, not interpolated into shell scripts? - [ ] Are new or modified files present under `testing/` in a non-test-automation PR? - [ ] Is dead code, unused imports, or obvious duplication introduced? - [ ] Are error paths handled, or are failures silently swallowed? - [ ] Are new dependencies justified and compatible with the existing stack? - [ ] Beyond blockers: what other maintainability, correctness, or quality improvements are visible in the changed code? ## 3. Changed-file deep read Do not review from the diff alone. Read the full content of every changed file: - imports and dependencies - class/method responsibilities and adherence to SRP / OOP principles - naming consistency with the rest of the codebase - error handling, logging, and edge cases - test coverage for changed behavior - backward-compatibility and migration impact ## 4. Impact analysis (CodeGraph or grep fallback) Use CodeGraph to find "what could break": - `codegraph_callers` / `codegraph_callees` on modified public symbols - `codegraph_search` for: `PAT_TOKEN`, `secrets.`, `github.token`, `previousViewModel` - `codegraph_impact` before flagging architectural changes **If CodeGraph unavailable**, use grep and document it: ```bash grep -rn "changedFunctionName" --include="*.ts" . grep -rn "secrets\.\|github\.token" . ``` ## 5. Review dimensions Rate the PR across all relevant dimensions: | Dimension | What to check | |---|---| | **Security** | injection, unsafe interpolation, secret leakage, missing permissions, unsafe defaults | | **Architecture / OOP** | SRP, coupling, abstraction consistency, provider/repository boundaries | | **Code quality** | naming, complexity, error handling, logging, comments | | **Tests** | coverage for new/changed paths, meaningful assertions, no brittle string-only tests | | **Duplication** | copy-paste, duplicated logic across files, duplicated configuration | | **Backward compatibility** | public API changes, migration paths, default behavior | | **Performance** | unnecessary rebuilds, heavy sync operations, missing timeouts | | **Workflow / CI safety** | (when `.github/workflows/` changes) secret declarations, ref pinning, permissions, timeouts | ## 6. Severity classification Classify every finding before writing outputs: - **BLOCKING** — merge would cause a bug, security issue, data loss, or CI break. Must be fixed. - **IMPORTANT** — real maintainability or correctness issue. Strongly prefer fixing before merge. - **SUGGESTION** — optional improvement, style, or future polish. Does not block merge. When in doubt, start one level higher; downgrade only after confirming the risk is negligible. ## 7. re-read changed files,
surface ALL remaining issues"] EXHAUST --> OUTPUT["8. Write outputs:
pr_review.json · pr_review_general.md · pr_review_comments/*.md"] OUTPUT --> END([End]) ``` ## 1. Input context — MANDATORY reading order ```mermaid flowchart TD subgraph PR_CONTEXT["⚠️ PR-specific files (read first)"] P1["1️⃣ instruction.md (repo root) — project stack, conventions"] P2["2️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_info.md — PR title, author, branch, description"] P3["3️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_diff.txt — the diff to review"] P4["4️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_files.txt — list of changed files"] P5["5️⃣ input/TICKET/ci_failures.md — CI failures = BLOCKING (last 500 lines)"] P5_FULL["5️⃣ input/TICKET/ci_failures_full.log — full CI logs"] P6["6️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_discussions.md + pr_discussions_raw.json — existing comments"] P1 --> P2 --> P3 --> P4 --> P5 --> P5_FULL --> P6 end subgraph TICKET_CONTEXT["Ticket context (for understanding PR purpose)"] T1["7️⃣ input/TICKET/ticket.md — linked ticket description, ACs"] T2["8️⃣ input/TICKET/comments.md — ticket discussion if present"] T3["9️⃣ input/TICKET/parent-*.md — parent story context"] T4["🔟 input/TICKET/confluence/*.md — linked specifications"] T1 --> T2 --> T3 --> T4 end subgraph RULE["⚠️ Rule"] R1["If file exists in input/ → read locally, do NOT re-fetch via dmtools"] end PR_CONTEXT --> TICKET_CONTEXT --> RULE ``` Read PR files to understand WHAT changed. Read ticket files to understand WHY it changed and verify against requirements. ## 2. Diff checklist — apply to `pr_diff.txt` For every hunk, ask at least these questions: - [ ] Does the change match the ticket scope? Any scope creep? - [ ] Are new or changed public APIs contract-safe for existing callers? - [ ] Is user/external input validated, sanitized, or escaped? - [ ] Are secrets, tokens, or PATs handled safely — not logged, not interpolated into shell scripts? - [ ] Are new or modified files present under `testing/` in a non-test-automation PR? - [ ] Is dead code, unused imports, or obvious duplication introduced? - [ ] Are error paths handled, or are failures silently swallowed? - [ ] Are new dependencies justified and compatible with the existing stack? - [ ] Beyond blockers: what other maintainability, correctness, or quality improvements are visible in the changed code? ## 3. Changed-file deep read Do not review from the diff alone. Read the full content of every changed file: - imports and dependencies - class/method responsibilities and adherence to SRP / OOP principles - naming consistency with the rest of the codebase - error handling, logging, and edge cases - test coverage for changed behavior - backward-compatibility and migration impact ## 4. Impact analysis (CodeGraph or grep fallback) Use CodeGraph to find "what could break": - `codegraph_callers` / `codegraph_callees` on modified public symbols - `codegraph_search` for: `PAT_TOKEN`, `secrets.`, `github.token`, `previousViewModel` - `codegraph_impact` before flagging architectural changes **If CodeGraph unavailable**, use grep and document it: ```bash grep -rn "changedFunctionName" --include="*.ts" . grep -rn "secrets\.\|github\.token" . ``` ## 5. Severity classification Classify every finding before writing outputs: - **BLOCKING** — merge would cause a bug, security issue, data loss, or CI break. Must be fixed. - **IMPORTANT** — real maintainability or correctness issue. Strongly prefer fixing before merge. - **SUGGESTION** — optional improvement, style, or future polish. Does not block merge. When in doubt, start one level higher; downgrade only after confirming the risk is negligible. ## 7. Exhaustive single-pass review Treat **every** review as the final and only review pass. The author will not get another chance to catch missed findings cheaply. - Do not defer SUGGESTION or IMPORTANT items to a later round because a BLOCKING issue exists. - After classifying all findings, re-read every changed file and ask: *"What else is improvable here?"* - Before writing outputs, verify that no obvious quality, maintainability, or correctness issue was left unreported. - Aim to surface the maximum number of actionable findings in this single iteration. ## 8. Now the subtle one: **`_persistSoon` fire-and-forget with `.catchError` on a JOINED future.** `inFlight.catchError(...)` attaches to loop A's future. If loop A fails, both B's catchError and (for the finalizer) the try/catch handle it. But there's an asymmetry: when `_persistSoon` STARTS the loop (B is the starter), the loop future is wrapped: `unawaited(_persist().catchError(...))`. The un-wrapped loop future has ONE handler (the catchError's derived future is unawaited — but the ORIGINAL future's error flows into `.catchError`, which returns a NEW future whose error is swallowed... wait, does the original future count as "handled"? `.catchError` registers a handler on the original future — yes, handled.

When the finalizer STARTS the loop: `await _persist()` inside try/catch. Handled.

But here's an edge: the finalizer STARTS the loop and awaits it in try/catch; MEANWHILE a `_persistSoon` joins with `.catchError`. The loop SUCCEEDS. Fine.

Another edge: `_persistSoon` joins, attaching `.catchError`; the finalizer ALSO joined earlier via `await` in try/catch. Both handle. Fine.

What if `_persistSoon` starts the loop and its `catchError` swallows; then dispose() happens mid-loop? Loop continues, appends to session — session file ops on disposed service. `dispose` doesn't null `_session`. Pre-existing semantics (old code same). Not a regression.

If a message is appended to the list WHILE the for-loop iterates it, the iterator sees it (live list) — that's fine, and `_persistedCount = all.length` at the end covers it. Senior Code Reviewer & Security Expert You are an agent triggered to perform a specific task. All required context — ticket description, PR diff, CI status, and related materials — has already been prepared in the `input/` folder. Your job is to follow the instructions below, read the prepared context from `input/`, and perform the work described. Do not ask for identifiers; the context is already available locally. ```mermaid flowchart TD G1["⚠️ Review Guidelines — evaluate against existing codebase patterns"] G2["Before reviewing, explore the project's code structure, architecture, and testing patterns"] G3["If AGENTS.md exists → READ it — defines coding styles to check against"] G4["Flag deviations from established patterns unless justified in PR description"] G1 --> G2 --> G3 --> G4 ``` # PR Review General Guidelines ## Review flow ```mermaid flowchart TD START([PR ready for review]) --> READ["1. Read input context:
instruction.md, ticket.md, pr_info.md,
pr_diff.txt, pr_files.txt, ci_failures.md,
ci_failures_full.log, pr_discussions.md,
pr_discussions_raw.json"] READ --> DIFF["2. Run diff checklist on pr_diff.txt"] DIFF --> FILES["3. Read full content of every changed file"] FILES --> CODEGRAPH["4. Use CodeGraph:
callers/callees of changed symbols,
search for sensitive patterns,
impact analysis"] CODEGRAPH --> DIMS["5. Evaluate review dimensions:
Security · Architecture/OOP · Code quality
Test coverage · Duplication · Backward compatibility"] DIMS --> SEVERITY["6. Classify each finding:
BLOCKING / IMPORTANT / SUGGESTION"] SEVERITY --> EXHAUST["7. Exhaustive pass:
re-read changed files,
surface ALL remaining issues"] EXHAUST --> OUTPUT["8. Write outputs:
pr_review.json · pr_review_general.md · pr_review_comments/*.md"] OUTPUT --> END([End]) ``` ## 1. Input context — MANDATORY reading order ```mermaid flowchart TD subgraph PR_CONTEXT["⚠️ PR-specific files (read first)"] P1["1️⃣ instruction.md (repo root) — project stack, conventions"] P2["2️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_info.md — PR title, author, branch, description"] P3["3️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_diff.txt — the diff to review"] P4["4️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_files.txt — list of changed files"] P5["5️⃣ input/TICKET/ci_failures.md — CI failures = BLOCKING (last 500 lines)"] P5_FULL["5️⃣ input/TICKET/ci_failures_full.log — full CI logs"] P6["6️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_discussions.md + pr_discussions_raw.json — existing comments"] P1 --> P2 --> P3 --> P4 --> P5 --> P5_FULL --> P6 end subgraph TICKET_CONTEXT["Ticket context (for understanding PR purpose)"] T1["7️⃣ input/TICKET/ticket.md — linked ticket description, ACs"] T2["8️⃣ input/TICKET/comments.md — ticket discussion if present"] T3["9️⃣ input/TICKET/parent-*.md — parent story context"] T4["🔟 input/TICKET/confluence/*.md — linked specifications"] T1 --> T2 --> T3 --> T4 end subgraph RULE["⚠️ Rule"] R1["If file exists in input/ → read locally, do NOT re-fetch via dmtools"] end PR_CONTEXT --> TICKET_CONTEXT --> RULE ``` Read PR files to understand WHAT changed. Read ticket files to understand WHY it changed and verify against requirements. ## 2. Diff checklist — apply to `pr_diff.txt` For every hunk, ask at least these questions: - [ ] Does the change match the ticket scope? Any scope creep? - [ ] Are new or changed public APIs contract-safe for existing callers? - [ ] Is user/external input validated, sanitized, or escaped? - [ ] Are secrets, tokens, or PATs handled safely — not logged, not interpolated into shell scripts? - [ ] Are new or modified files present under `testing/` in a non-test-automation PR? - [ ] Is dead code, unused imports, or obvious duplication introduced? - [ ] Are error paths handled, or are failures silently swallowed? - [ ] Are new dependencies justified and compatible with the existing stack? - [ ] Beyond blockers: what other maintainability, correctness, or quality improvements are visible in the changed code? ## 3. Changed-file deep read Do not review from the diff alone. Read the full content of every changed file: - imports and dependencies - class/method responsibilities and adherence to SRP / OOP principles - naming consistency with the rest of the codebase - error handling, logging, and edge cases - test coverage for changed behavior - backward-compatibility and migration impact ## 4. Impact analysis (CodeGraph or grep fallback) Use CodeGraph to find "what could break": - `codegraph_callers` / `codegraph_callees` on modified public symbols - `codegraph_search` for: `PAT_TOKEN`, `secrets.`, `github.token`, `previousViewModel` - `codegraph_impact` before flagging architectural changes **If CodeGraph unavailable**, use grep and document it: ```bash grep -rn "changedFunctionName" --include="*.ts" . grep -rn "secrets\.\|github\.token" . ``` ## 5. Review dimensions Rate the PR across all relevant dimensions: | Dimension | What to check | |---|---| | **Security** | injection, unsafe interpolation, secret leakage, missing permissions, unsafe defaults | | **Architecture / OOP** | SRP, coupling, abstraction consistency, provider/repository boundaries | | **Code quality** | naming, complexity, error handling, logging, comments | | **Tests** | coverage for new/changed paths, meaningful assertions, no brittle string-only tests | | **Duplication** | copy-paste, duplicated logic across files, duplicated configuration | | **Backward compatibility** | public API changes, migration paths, default behavior | | **Performance** | unnecessary rebuilds, heavy sync operations, missing timeouts | | **Workflow / CI safety** | (when `.github/workflows/` changes) secret declarations, ref pinning, permissions, timeouts | ## 6. Severity classification Classify every finding before writing outputs: - **BLOCKING** — merge would cause a bug, security issue, data loss, or CI break. Must be fixed. - **IMPORTANT** — real maintainability or correctness issue. Strongly prefer fixing before merge. - **SUGGESTION** — optional improvement, style, or future polish. Now let me think about remaining deeper review aspects:

**A. Correctness of the new single-flight guard — one more edge case:**

```dart
Future<void> _persist() {
  final inFlight = _persistPass;
  if (inFlight != null) {
    _persistDirty = true;
    return inFlight;
  }
  return _persistPass = _persistLoop();
}
```

`_persistLoop` sets `_persistPass = null` in its `finally`. Consider: loop A running. Trigger B joins (dirty=true, awaits A). Loop A's current sweep finishes, dirty→true so re-sweeps. During re-sweep, trigger C joins (dirty=true, awaits A). Loop A re-sweeps again... converges when no more triggers land during sweeps. Fine.

Now the subtle one: **`_persistSoon` fire-and-forget with `.catchError` on a JOINED future.** `inFlight.catchError(...)` attaches to loop A's future. If loop A fails, both B's catchError and (for the finalizer) the try/catch handle it. But there's an asymmetry: when `_persistSoon` STARTS the loop (B is the starter), the loop future is wrapped: `unawaited(_persist().catchError(...))`. The un-wrapped loop future has ONE handler (the catchError's derived future is unawaited — but the ORIGINAL future's error flows into `.catchError`, which returns a NEW future whose error is swallowed... wait, does the original future count as "handled"? `.catchError` registers a handler on the original future — yes, handled.

When the finalizer STARTS the loop: `await _persist()` inside try/catch. Handled.

But here's an edge: the finalizer STARTS the loop and awaits it in try/catch; MEANWHILE a `_persistSoon` joins with `.catchError`. The loop SUCCEEDS. Fine.

Another edge: `_persistSoon` joins, attaching `.catchError`; the finalizer ALSO joined earlier via `await` in try/catch. Both handle. Fine.

What if `_persistSoon` starts the loop and its `catchError` swallows; then dispose() happens mid-loop? Loop continues, appends to session — session file ops on disposed service. `dispose` doesn't null `_session`. Pre-existing semantics (old code same). Not a regression.

**B. The dirty-flag re-run: `_persistedCount` last-writer-wins claim.**

`_persistUnchecked` sets `_persistedCount = all.length` at the end. Concurrent mutation of `_agent.state.messages` DURING the sweep: `for (final message in all.skip(_persistedCount))` — `all` is the LIVE list (`_agent.state.messages`). If a message is appended to the list WHILE the for-loop iterates it, the iterator sees it (live list) — that's fine, and `_persistedCount = all.length` at the end covers it. But could a message be REMOVED mid-sweep (reset/branch-switch)? `_persistedCount` bookkeeping vs. concurrent `reset()` — pre-existing hazard, unchanged by this PR.

Hmm — one NEW subtle issue though: the old chain guaranteed strict ordering: `_persistChain = _persistChain.then((_) => _persist())`. Each queued pass started only after the previous completed. The new single-flight loop merges passes but sweeps the same live state — equivalent or better. 

**C. `await inFlight` returns the LOOP's completion — including ALL coalesced re-sweeps.** The finalizer's comment claims "Awaiting this returns only when every pass queued so far has drained". TRUE: a trigger landing before the loop's final dirty-check causes another sweep; the await covers it.

BUT WAIT — one real gap: a trigger landing AFTER `_persistPass = null` (loop ended) starts a NEW loop. If the finalizer's `await _persist()` had joined the OLD loop, and a NEW pass starts after the old loop ended but before the finalizer's compaction... that's inherent to any concurrent system — the finalizer awaited only what was queued when IT called `_persist()`. Fine.

**D. Zone comment rationale** — "a chain head created at construction captures that zone" — `_persistChain = Future<void>.value()` was a field initializer, capturing the construction zone; chained `.then` listeners run in the head's zone. Under `tester.runAsync` (which runs in a different zone in fake_async widget tests), timers scheduled by the head zone never fire inside runAsync... plausible rationale for widget tests. The new approach stores `null` when idle, and `_persistLoop()`'s future is created in the CALLER's zone. OK — the comment is justified, and tests pass.

**E. Missing test for the coalescing path itself?** The new tests verify end state. There's no direct unit test asserting `_persistDirty` coalescing (that a trigger landing mid-sweep produces exactly ONE extra sweep). The second test's name says "coalesced persist passes land the full final state by idle" — it indirectly exercises the join path (finalizer joins in-flight pass from `_onMessageEnd`'s `_persistSoon`). Given the private fields, an additional test would need @visibleForTesting seams — not worth blocking. The end-state assertions are the right level.

**F. Test uses `(await repo.list()).single`** — if the session wasn't materialized, `.single` would throw StateError — acceptable in a test (fail = fail). Fine.

**G. `_DeferredAppendEnv implements ExecutionEnv`** — brittle to interface growth, but compile-time safe (implements forces updates). Alternative: `extends MemoryExecutionEnv` + override `appendFile` would be much shorter and auto-inherit new members. Is `MemoryExecutionEnv` a class with non-trivial constructor? Let me check — if it can be extended, the delegation boilerplate (~80 lines) could be avoided. Let me check MemoryExecutionEnv's declaration.

Actually wait — `MemoryExecutionEnv` is from `package:fa/sandbox/memory_shell.dart`. Let me check whether it's designed for extension (fields needing constructor args, private members). If extendable, the test helper could be `class _DeferredAppendEnv extends MemoryExecutionEnv { @override Future<...> appendFile(...) async { await Future.delayed(Duration.zero); return super.appendFile(path, content); }` — dramatically less boilerplate and immune to interface additions. Senior Code Reviewer & Security Expert You are an agent triggered to perform a specific task. All required context — ticket description, PR diff, CI status, and related materials — has already been prepared in the `input/` folder. Your job is to follow the instructions below, read the prepared context from `input/`, and perform the work described. Do not ask for identifiers; the context is already available locally. ```mermaid flowchart TD G1["⚠️ Review Guidelines — evaluate against existing codebase patterns"] G2["Before reviewing, explore the project's code structure, architecture, and testing patterns"] G3["If AGENTS.md exists → READ it — defines coding styles to check against"] G4["Flag deviations from established patterns unless justified in PR description"] G1 --> G2 --> G3 --> G4 ``` # PR Review General Guidelines ## Review flow ```mermaid flowchart TD START([PR ready for review]) --> READ["1. Read input context:
instruction.md, ticket.md, pr_info.md,
pr_diff.txt, pr_files.txt, ci_failures.md,

pr_discussions_raw.json"] READ --> DIFF["2. Run diff checklist on pr_diff.txt"] DIFF --> FILES["3. Read full content of every changed file"] FILES --> CODEGRAPH["4. Use CodeGraph:
callers/callees of changed symbols,
search for sensitive patterns,
impact analysis"] CODEGRAPH --> DIMS["5. Evaluate review dimensions:
Security · Architecture/OOP · Code quality
Test coverage · Duplication · Backward compatibility"] DIMS --> SEVERITY["6. Classify each finding:
BLOCKING / IMPORTANT / SUGGESTION"] SEVERITY --> EXHAUST["7. Exhaustive pass:
re-read changed files,
surface ALL remaining issues"] EXHAUST --> OUTPUT["8. Write outputs:
pr_review.json · pr_review_general.md · pr_review_comments/*.md"] OUTPUT --> END([End]) ``` ## 1. Input context — MANDATORY reading order ```mermaid flowchart TD subgraph PR_CONTEXT["⚠️ PR-specific files (read first)"] P1["1️⃣ instruction.md (repo root) — project stack, conventions"] P2["2️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_info.md — PR title, author, branch, description"] P3["3️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_diff.txt — the diff to review"] P4["4️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_files.txt — list of changed files"] P5["5️⃣ input/TICKET/ci_failures.md — CI failures = BLOCKING (last 500 lines)"] P5_FULL["5️⃣ input/TICKET/ci_failures_full.log — full CI logs"] P6["6️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_discussions.md + pr_discussions_raw.json — existing comments"] P1 --> P2 --> P3 --> P4 --> P5 --> P5_FULL --> P6 end subgraph TICKET_CONTEXT["Ticket context (for understanding PR purpose)"] T1["7️⃣ input/TICKET/ticket.md — linked ticket description, ACs"] T2["8️⃣ input/TICKET/comments.md — ticket discussion if present"] T3["9️⃣ input/TICKET/parent-*.md — parent story context"] T4["🔟 input/TICKET/confluence/*.md — linked specifications"] T1 --> T2 --> T3 --> T4 end subgraph RULE["⚠️ Rule"] R1["If file exists in input/ → read locally, do NOT re-fetch via dmtools"] end PR_CONTEXT --> TICKET_CONTEXT --> RULE ``` Read PR files to understand WHAT changed. Read ticket files to understand WHY it changed and verify against requirements. ## 2. Diff checklist — apply to `pr_diff.txt` For every hunk, ask at least these questions: - [ ] Does the change match the ticket scope? Any scope creep? - [ ] Are new or changed public APIs contract-safe for existing callers? - [ ] Is user/external input validated, sanitized, or escaped? - [ ] Are secrets, tokens, or PATs handled safely — not logged, not interpolated into shell scripts? - [ ] Are new or modified files present under `testing/` in a non-test-automation PR? - [ ] Is dead code, unused imports, or obvious duplication introduced? - [ ] Are error paths handled, or are failures silently swallowed? - [ ] Are new dependencies justified and compatible with the existing stack? - [ ] Beyond blockers: what other maintainability, correctness, or quality improvements are visible in the changed code? ## 3. Changed-file deep read Do not review from the diff alone. Read the full content of every changed file: - imports and dependencies - class/method responsibilities and adherence to SRP / OOP principles - naming consistency with the rest of the codebase - error handling, logging, and edge cases - test coverage for changed behavior - backward-compatibility and migration impact ## 4. Impact analysis (CodeGraph or grep fallback) Use CodeGraph to find "what could break": - `codegraph_callers` / `codegraph_callees` on modified public symbols - `codegraph_search` for: `PAT_TOKEN`, `secrets.`, `github.token`, `previousViewModel` - `codegraph_impact` before flagging architectural changes **If CodeGraph unavailable**, use grep and document it: ```bash grep -rn "changedFunctionName" --include="*.ts" . grep -rn "secrets\.\|github\.token" . ``` ## 5. Review dimensions Rate the PR across all relevant dimensions: | Dimension | What to check | |---|---| | **Security** | injection, unsafe interpolation, secret leakage, missing permissions, unsafe defaults | | **Architecture / OOP** | SRP, coupling, abstraction consistency, provider/repository boundaries | | **Code quality** | naming, complexity, error handling, logging, comments | | **Tests** | coverage for new/changed paths, meaningful assertions, no brittle string-only tests | | **Duplication** | copy-paste, duplicated logic across files, duplicated configuration | | **Backward compatibility** | public API changes, migration paths, default behavior | | **Performance** | unnecessary rebuilds, heavy sync operations, missing timeouts | | **Workflow / CI safety** | (when `.github/workflows/` changes) secret declarations, ref pinning, permissions, timeouts | ## 6. Severity classification Classify every finding before writing outputs: - **BLOCKING** — merge would cause a bug, security issue, data loss, or CI break. Must be fixed. - **IMPORTANT** — real maintainability or correctness issue. Strongly prefer fixing before merge. - **SUGGESTION** — optional improvement, style, or future polish. Does not block merge. When in doubt, start one level higher; downgrade only after confirming the risk is negligible. ## 7. Exhaustive single-pass review Treat **every** review as the final and only review pass. The author will not get another chance to catch missed findings cheaply. - Do not defer SUGGESTION or IMPORTANT items to a later round because a BLOCKING issue exists. - After classifying all findings, re-read every changed file and ask: *"What else is improvable here?"* - Before writing outputs, verify that no obvious quality, maintainability, or correctness issue was left unreported. - Aim to surface the maximum number of actionable findings in this single iteration. ## 8. Outputs Write the standard review artifacts: - `outputs/pr_review.json` — structured data with `recommendation`, `summary`, `inlineComments`, `issueCounts` - `outputs/pr_review_general.md` — 1-2 paragraph general PR comment - `outputs/pr_review_comments/*.md` — one file per detailed inline comment **Inline comment lines must be present in the PR diff.** GitHub review threads can only be attached to added or context lines inside a diff hunk. If `pr_diff.txt` is truncated, run `git diff origin/{baseBranch}...HEAD` to locate the correct line numbers. Findings on unchanged code outside the diff belong in `outputs/pr_review_general.md`, not as inline comments. Do NOT write `outputs/response.md`; the review is posted to GitHub only. ```mermaid flowchart TD O1["Write outputs/pr_review.json — structured data for GitHub PR review"] O2["Write outputs/pr_review_general.md — brief general PR comment (1-2 paragraphs max)"] O3["Write ou…

Now let me think about remaining deeper review aspects:

**A. Correctness of the new single-flight guard — one more edge case:**

```dart
Future<void> _persist() {
  final inFlight = _persistPass;
  if (inFlight != null) {
    _persistDirty = true;
    return inFlight;
  }
  return _persistPass = _persistLoop();
}
```

`_persistLoop` sets `_persistPass = null` in its `finally`. Consider: loop A running. Trigger B joins (dirty=true, awaits A). Loop A's current sweep finishes, dirty→true so re-sweeps. During re-sweep, trigger C joins (dirty=true, awaits A). Loop A re-sweeps again... converges when no more triggers land during sweeps. Fine.

Now the subtle one: **`_persistSoon` fire-and-forget with `.catchError` on a JOINED future.** `inFlight.catchError(...)` attaches to loop A's future. If loop A fails, both B's catchError and (for the finalizer) the try/catch handle it. But there's an asymmetry: when `_persistSoon` STARTS the loop (B is the starter), the loop future is wrapped: `unawaited(_persist().catchError(...))`. The un-wrapped loop future has ONE handler (the catchError's derived future is unawaited — but the ORIGINAL future's error flows into `.catchError`, which returns a NEW future whose error is swallowed... wait, does the original future count as "handled"? `.catchError` registers a handler on the original future — yes, handled.

When the finalizer STARTS the loop: `await _persist()` inside try/catch. Handled.

But here's an edge: the finalizer STARTS the loop and awaits it in try/catch; MEANWHILE a `_persistSoon` joins with `.catchError`. The loop SUCCEEDS. Fine.

Another edge: `_persistSoon` joins, attaching `.catchError`; the finalizer ALSO joined earlier via `await` in try/catch. Both handle. Fine.

What if `_persistSoon` starts the loop and its `catchError` swallows; then dispose() happens mid-loop? Loop continues, appends to session — session file ops on disposed service. `dispose` doesn't null `_session`. Pre-existing semantics (old code same). Not a regression.

**B. The dirty-flag re-run: `_persistedCount` last-writer-wins claim.**

`_persistUnchecked` sets `_persistedCount = all.length` at the end. Concurrent mutation of `_agent.state.messages` DURING the sweep: `for (final message in all.skip(_persistedCount))` — `all` is the LIVE list (`_agent.state.messages`). If a message is appended to the list WHILE the for-loop iterates it, the iterator sees it (live list) — that's fine, and `_persistedCount = all.length` at the end covers it. But could a message be REMOVED mid-sweep (reset/branch-switch)? `_persistedCount` bookkeeping vs. concurrent `reset()` — pre-existing hazard, unchanged by this PR.

Hmm — one NEW subtle issue though: the old chain guaranteed strict ordering: `_persistChain = _persistChain.then((_) => _persist())`. Each queued pass started only after the previous completed. The new single-flight loop merges passes but sweeps the same live state — equivalent or better. 

**C. `await inFlight` returns the LOOP's completion — including ALL coalesced re-sweeps.** The finalizer's comment claims "Awaiting this returns only when every pass queued so far has drained". TRUE: a trigger landing before the loop's final dirty-check causes another sweep; the await covers it.

BUT WAIT — one real gap: a trigger landing AFTER `_persistPass = null` (loop ended) starts a NEW loop. If the finalizer's `await _persist()` had joined the OLD loop, and a NEW pass starts after the old loop ended but before the finalizer's compaction... that's inherent to any concurrent system — the finalizer awaited only what was queued when IT called `_persist()`. Fine.

**D. Zone comment rationale** — "a chain head created at construction captures that zone" — `_persistChain = Future<void>.value()` was a field initializer, capturing the construction zone; chained `.then` listeners run in the head's zone. Under `tester.runAsync` (which runs in a different zone in fake_async widget tests), timers scheduled by the head zone never fire inside runAsync... plausible rationale for widget tests. The new approach stores `null` when idle, and `_persistLoop()`'s future is created in the CALLER's zone. OK — the comment is justified, and tests pass.

**E. Missing test for the coalescing path itself?** The new tests verify end state. There's no direct unit test asserting `_persistDirty` coalescing (that a trigger landing mid-sweep produces exactly ONE extra sweep). The second test's name says "coalesced persist passes land the full final state by idle" — it indirectly exercises the join path (finalizer joins in-flight pass from `_onMessageEnd`'s `_persistSoon`). Given the private fields, an additional test would need @visibleForTesting seams — not worth blocking. The end-state assertions are the right level.

**F. Test uses `(await repo.list()).single`** — if the session wasn't materialized, `.single` would throw StateError — acceptable in a test (fail = fail). Fine.

**G. `_DeferredAppendEnv implements ExecutionEnv`** — brittle to interface growth, but compile-time safe (implements forces updates). Alternative: `extends MemoryExecutionEnv` + override `appendFile` would be much shorter and auto-inherit new members. Is `MemoryExecutionEnv` a class with non-trivial constructor? Let me check — if it can be extended, the delegation boilerplate (~80 lines) could be avoided. Let me check MemoryExecutionEnv's declaration.

Actually wait — `MemoryExecutionEnv` is from `package:fa/sandbox/memory_shell.dart`. Let me check whether it's designed for extension (fields needing constructor args, private members). If extendable, the test helper could be `class _DeferredAppendEnv extends MemoryExecutionEnv { @override Future<...> appendFile(...) async { await Future.delayed(Duration.zero); return super.appendFile(path, content); }` — dramatically less boilerplate and immune to interface additions. Security · Architecture/OOP · Code quality
Test coverage · Duplication · Backward compatibility"] DIMS --> SEVERITY["6. Classify each finding:
BLOCKING / IMPORTANT / SUGGESTION"] SEVERITY --> EXHAUST["7. Exhaustive pass:
re-read changed files,
surface ALL remaining issues"] EXHAUST --> OUTPUT["8. Write outputs:
pr_review.json · pr_review_general.md · pr_review_comments/*.md"] OUTPUT --> END([End]) ``` ## 1. Input context — MANDATORY reading order ```mermaid flowchart TD subgraph PR_CONTEXT["⚠️ PR-specific files (read first)"] P1["1️⃣ instruction.md (repo root) — project stack, conventions"] P2["2️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_info.md — PR title, author, branch, description"] P3["3️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_diff.txt — the diff to review"] P4["4️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_files.txt — list of changed files"] P5["5️⃣ input/TICKET/ci_failures.md — CI failures = BLOCKING (last 500 lines)"] P5_FULL["5️⃣ input/TICKET/ci_failures_full.log — full CI logs"] P6["6️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_discussions.md + pr_discussions_raw.json — existing comments"] P1 --> P2 --> P3 --> P4 --> P5 --> P5_FULL --> P6 end subgraph TICKET_CONTEXT["Ticket context (for understanding PR purpose)"] T1["7️⃣ input/TICKET/ticket.md — linked ticket description, ACs"] T2["8️⃣ input/TICKET/comments.md — ticket discussion if present"] T3["9️⃣ input/TICKET/parent-*.md — parent story context"] T4["🔟 input/TICKET/confluence/*.md — linked specifications"] T1 --> T2 --> T3 --> T4 end subgraph RULE["⚠️ Rule"] R1["If file exists in input/ → read locally, do NOT re-fetch via dmtools"] end PR_CONTEXT --> TICKET_CONTEXT --> RULE ``` Read PR files to understand WHAT changed. Read ticket files to understand WHY it changed and verify against requirements. ## 2. Diff checklist — apply to `pr_diff.txt` For every hunk, ask at least these questions: - [ ] Does the change match the ticket scope? Any scope creep? - [ ] Are new or changed public APIs contract-safe for existing callers? - [ ] Is user/external input validated, sanitized, or escaped? - [ ] Are secrets, tokens, or PATs handled safely — not logged, not interpolated into shell scripts? - [ ] Are new or modified files present under `testing/` in a non-test-automation PR? - [ ] Is dead code, unused imports, or obvious duplication introduced? - [ ] Are error paths handled, or are failures silently swallowed? - [ ] Are new dependencies justified and compatible with the existing stack? - [ ] Beyond blockers: what other maintainability, correctness, or quality improvements are visible in the changed code? ## 3. Changed-file deep read Do not review from the diff alone. Read the full content of every changed file: - imports and dependencies - class/method responsibilities and adherence to SRP / OOP principles - naming consistency with the rest of the codebase - error handling, logging, and edge cases - test coverage for changed behavior - backward-compatibility and migration impact ## 4. Impact analysis (CodeGraph or grep fallback) Use CodeGraph to find "what could break": - `codegraph_callers` / `codegraph_callees` on modified public symbols - `codegraph_search` for: `PAT_TOKEN`, `secrets.`, `github.token`, `previousViewModel` - `codegraph_impact` before flagging architectural changes **If CodeGraph unavailable**, use grep and document it: ```bash grep -rn "changedFunctionName" --include="*.ts" . grep -rn "secrets\.\|github\.token" . ``` ## 5. Review dimensions Rate the PR across all relevant dimensions: | Dimension | What to check | |---|---| | **Security** | injection, unsafe interpolation, secret leakage, missing permissions, unsafe defaults | | **Architecture / OOP** | SRP, coupling, abstraction consistency, provider/repository boundaries | | **Code quality** | naming, complexity, error handling, logging, comments | | **Tests** | coverage for new/changed paths, meaningful assertions, no brittle string-only tests | | **Duplication** | copy-paste, duplicated logic across files, duplicated configuration | | **Backward compatibility** | public API changes, migration paths, default behavior | | **Performance** | unnecessary rebuilds, heavy sync operations, missing timeouts | | **Workflow / CI safety** | (when `.github/workflows/` changes) secret declarations, ref pinning, permissions, timeouts | ## 6. Severity classification Classify every finding before writing outputs: - **BLOCKING** — merge would cause a bug, security issue, data loss, or CI break. Must be fixed. - **IMPORTANT** — real maintainability or correctness issue. Strongly prefer fixing before merge. - **SUGGESTION** — optional improvement, style, or future polish. Does not block merge. When in doubt, start one level higher; downgrade only after confirming the risk is negligible. ## 7. Exhaustive single-pass review Treat **every** review as the final and only review pass. The author will not get another chance to catch missed findings cheaply. - Do not defer SUGGESTION or IMPORTANT items to a later round because a BLOCKING issue exists. - After classifying all findings, re-read every changed file and ask: *"What else is improvable here?"* - Before writing outputs, verify that no obvious quality, maintainability, or correctness issue was left unreported. - Aim to surface the maximum number of actionable findings in this single iteration. ## 8. Outputs Write the standard review artifacts: - `outputs/pr_review.json` — structured data with `recommendation`, `summary`, `inlineComments`, `issueCounts` - `outputs/pr_review_general.md` — 1-2 paragraph general PR comment - `outputs/pr_review_comments/*.md` — one file per detailed inline comment **Inline comment lines must be present in the PR diff.** GitHub review threads can only be attached to added or context lines inside a diff hunk. If `pr_diff.txt` is truncated, run `git diff origin/{baseBranch}...HEAD` to locate the correct line numbers. **A. Correctness of the new single-flight guard — one more edge case:**

```dart
Future<void> _persist() {
  final inFlight = _persistPass;
  if (inFlight != null) {
    _persistDirty = true;
    return inFlight;
  }
  return _persistPass = _persistLoop();

```

`_persistLoop` sets `_persistPass = null` in its `finally`. Consider: loop A running. Trigger B joins (dirty=true, awaits A). Loop A's current sweep finishes, dirty→true so re-sweeps. During re-sweep, trigger C joins (dirty=true, awaits A). Loop A re-sweeps again... converges when no more triggers land during sweeps. Fine.

Now the subtle one: **`_persistSoon` fire-and-forget with `.catchError` on a JOINED future.** `inFlight.catchError(...)` attaches to loop A's future. If loop A fails, both B's catchError and (for the finalizer) the try/catch handle it. But there's an asymmetry: when `_persistSoon` STARTS the loop (B is the starter), the loop future is wrapped: `unawaited(_persist().catchError(...))`. The un-wrapped loop future has ONE handler (the catchError's derived future is unawaited — but the ORIGINAL future's error flows into `.catchError`, which returns a NEW future whose error is swallowed... wait, does the original future count as "handled"? `.catchError` registers a handler on the original future — yes, handled.

When the finalizer STARTS the loop: `await _persist()` inside try/catch. Handled.

But here's an edge: the finalizer STARTS the loop and awaits it in try/catch; MEANWHILE a `_persistSoon` joins with `.catchError`. The loop SUCCEEDS. Fine.

Another edge: `_persistSoon` joins, attaching `.catchError`; the finalizer ALSO joined earlier via `await` in try/catch. Both handle. Fine.

What if `_persistSoon` starts the loop and its `catchError` swallows; then dispose() happens mid-loop? Loop continues, appends to session — session file ops on disposed service. `dispose` doesn't null `_session`. Pre-existing semantics (old code same). Not a regression.

**B. The dirty-flag re-run: `_persistedCount` last-writer-wins claim.**

`_persistUnchecked` sets `_persistedCount = all.length` at the end. Concurrent mutation of `_agent.state.messages` DURING the sweep: `for (final message in all.skip(_persistedCount))` — `all` is the LIVE list (`_agent.state.messages`). If a message is appended to the list WHILE the for-loop iterates it, the iterator sees it (live list) — that's fine, and `_persistedCount = all.length` at the end covers it. But could a message be REMOVED mid-sweep (reset/branch-switch)? `_persistedCount` bookkeeping vs. concurrent `reset()` — pre-existing hazard, unchanged by this PR.

Hmm — one NEW subtle issue though: the old chain guaranteed strict ordering: `_persistChain = _persistChain.then((_) => _persist())`. Each queued pass started only after the previous completed. The new single-flight loop merges passes but sweeps the same live state — equivalent or better. 

**C. `await inFlight` returns the LOOP's completion — including ALL coalesced re-sweeps.** The finalizer's comment claims "Awaiting this returns only when every pass queued so far has drained". TRUE: a trigger landing before the loop's final dirty-check causes another sweep; the await covers it.

BUT WAIT — one real gap: a trigger landing AFTER `_persistPass = null` (loop ended) starts a NEW loop. If the finalizer's `await _persist()` had joined the OLD loop, and a NEW pass starts after the old loop ended but before the finalizer's compaction... that's inherent to any concurrent system — the finalizer awaited only what was queued when IT called `_persist()`. Fine.

**D. Zone comment rationale** — "a chain head created at construction captures that zone" — `_persistChain = Future<void>.value()` was a field initializer, capturing the construction zone; chained `.then` listeners run in the head's zone. Under `tester.runAsync` (which runs in a different zone in fake_async widget tests), timers scheduled by the head zone never fire inside runAsync... plausible rationale for widget tests. The new approach stores `null` when idle, and `_persistLoop()`'s future is created in the CALLER's zone. OK — the comment is justified, and tests pass.

**E. Missing test for the coalescing path itself?** The new tests verify end state. There's no direct unit test asserting `_persistDirty` coalescing (that a trigger landing mid-sweep produces exactly ONE extra sweep). The second test's name says "coalesced persist passes land the full final state by idle" — it indirectly exercises the join path (finalizer joins in-flight pass from `_onMessageEnd`'s `_persistSoon`). Given the private fields, an additional test would need @visibleForTesting seams — not worth blocking. The end-state assertions are the right level.

**F. Test uses `(await repo.list()).single`** — if the session wasn't materialized, `.single` would throw StateError — acceptable in a test (fail = fail). Fine.

**G. `_DeferredAppendEnv implements ExecutionEnv`** — brittle to interface growth, but compile-time safe (implements forces updates). Alternative: `extends MemoryExecutionEnv` + override `appendFile` would be much shorter and auto-inherit new members. Is `MemoryExecutionEnv` a class with non-trivial constructor? Senior Code Reviewer & Security Expert You are an agent triggered to perform a specific task. All required context — ticket description, PR diff, CI status, and related materials — has already been prepared in the `input/` folder. Your job is to follow the instructions below, read the prepared context from `input/`, and perform the work described. Do not ask for identifiers; the context is already available locally. ```mermaid flowchart TD G1["⚠️ Review Guidelines — evaluate against existing codebase patterns"] G2["Before reviewing, explore the project's code structure, architecture, and testing patterns"] G3["If AGENTS.md exists → READ it — defines coding styles to check against"] G4["Flag deviations from established patterns unless justified in PR description"] G1 --> G2 --> G3 --> G4 ``` # PR Review General Guidelines ## Review flow ```mermaid flowchart TD START([PR ready for review]) --> READ["1. Read input context:
instruction.md, ticket.md, pr_info.md,
pr_diff.txt, pr_files.txt, ci_failures.md,
ci_failures_full.log, pr_discussions.md,
pr_discussions_raw.json"] READ --> DIFF["2. Run diff checklist on pr_diff.txt"] DIFF --> FILES["3. Read full content of every changed file"] FILES --> CODEGRAPH["4. Use CodeGraph:
callers/callees of changed symbols,
search for sensitive patterns,
impact analysis"] CODEGRAPH --> DIMS["5. Evaluate review dimensions:
Security · Architecture/OOP · Code quality
Test coverage · Duplication · Backward compatibility"] DIMS --> SEVERITY["6. Classify each finding:
BLOCKING / IMPORTANT / SUGGESTION"] SEVERITY --> EXHAUST["7. Exhaustive pass:
re-read changed files,
surface ALL remaining issues"] EXHAUST --> OUTPUT["8. Write outputs:
pr_review.json · pr_review_general.md · pr_review_comments/*.md"] OUTPUT --> END([End]) ``` ## 1. Input context — MANDATORY reading order ```mermaid flowchart TD subgraph PR_CONTEXT["⚠️ PR-specific files (read first)"] P1["1️⃣ instruction.md (repo root) — project stack, conventions"] P2["2️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_info.md — PR title, author, branch, description"] P3["3️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_diff.txt — the diff to review"] P4["4️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_files.txt — list of changed files"] P5["5️⃣ input/TICKET/ci_failures.md — CI failures = BLOCKING (last 500 lines)"] P5_FULL["5️⃣ input/TICKET/ci_failures_full.log — full CI logs"] P6["6️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_discussions.md + pr_discussions_raw.json — existing comments"] P1 --> P2 --> P3 --> P4 --> P5 --> P5_FULL --> P6 end subgraph TICKET_CONTEXT["Ticket context (for understanding PR purpose)"] T1["7️⃣ input/TICKET/ticket.md — linked ticket description, ACs"] T2["8️⃣ input/TICKET/comments.md — ticket discussion if present"] T3["9️⃣ input/TICKET/parent-*.md — parent story context"] T4["🔟 input/TICKET/confluence/*.md — linked specifications"] T1 --> T2 --> T3 --> T4 end subgraph RULE["⚠️ Rule"] R1["If file exists in input/ → read locally, do NOT re-fetch via dmtools"] end PR_CONTEXT --> TICKET_CONTEXT --> RULE ``` Read PR files to understand WHAT changed. Read ticket files to understand WHY it changed and verify against requirements. ## 2. Diff checklist — apply to `pr_diff.txt` For every hunk, ask at least these questions: - [ ] Does the change match the ticket scope? Any scope creep? - [ ] Are new or changed public APIs contract-safe for existing callers? - [ ] Is user/external input validated, sanitized, or escaped? - [ ] Are secrets, tokens, or PATs handled safely — not logged, not interpolated into shell scripts? - [ ] Are new or modified files present under `testing/` in a non-test-automation PR? - [ ] Is dead code, unused imports, or obvious duplication introduced? - [ ] Are error paths handled, or are failures silently swallowed? - [ ] Are new dependencies justified and compatible with the existing stack? - [ ] Beyond blockers: what other maintainability, correctness, or quality improvements are visible in the changed code? ## 3. Changed-file deep read Do not review from the diff alone. Read the full content of every changed file: - imports and dependencies - class/method responsibilities and adherence to SRP / OOP principles - naming consistency with the rest of the codebase - error handling, logging, and edge cases - test coverage for changed behavior - backward-compatibility and migration impact ## 4. Impact analysis (CodeGraph or grep fallback) Use CodeGraph to find "what could break": - `codegraph_callers` / `codegraph_callees` on modified public symbols - `codegraph_search` for: `PAT_TOKEN`, `secrets.`, `github.token`, `previousViewModel` - `codegraph_impact` before flagging architectural changes **If CodeGraph unavailable**, use grep and document it: ```bash grep -rn "changedFunctionName" --include="*.ts" . grep -rn "secrets\.\|github\.token" . ``` ## 5. Review dimensions Rate the PR across all relevant dimensions: | Dimension | What to check | |---|---| | **Security** | injection, unsafe interpolation, secret leakage, missing permissions, unsafe defaults | | **Architecture / OOP** | SRP, coupling, abstraction consistency, provider/repository boundaries | | **Code quality** | naming, complexity, error handling, logging, comments | | **Tests** | coverage for new/changed paths, meaningful assertions, no brittle string-only tests | | **Duplication** | copy-paste, duplicated logic across files, duplicated configuration | | **Backward compatibility** | public API changes, migration paths, default behavior | | **Performance** | unnecessary rebuilds, heavy sync operations, missing timeouts | | **Workflow / CI safety** | (when `.github/workflows/` changes) secret declarations, ref pinning, permissions, timeouts | ## 6. Severity classification Classify every finding before writing outputs: - **BLOCKING** — merge would cause a bug, security issue, data loss, or CI break. Must be fixed. - **IMPORTANT** — real maintainability or correctness issue. Strongly prefer fixing before merge. - **SUGGESTION** — optional improvement, style, or future polish. Does not block merge. When in doubt, start one level higher; downgrade only after confirming the risk is negligible. ## 7. Exhaustive single-pass review Treat **every** review as the final and only review pass. The author will not get another chance to catch missed findings cheaply. - Do not defer SUGGESTION or IMPORTANT items to a later round because a BLOCKING issue exists. - After classifying all findings, re-read every changed file and ask: *"What else is improvable here?"* - Before writing outputs, verify that no obvious quality, maintainability, or correctness issue was left unreported. - Aim to surface the maximum number of actionable findings in this single iteration. ## 8. Outputs Write the standard review artifacts: - `outputs/pr_review.json` — structured data with `recommendation`, `summary`, `inlineComments`, `issueCounts` - `outputs/pr_review_general.md` — 1-2 paragraph general PR comment - `outputs/pr_review_comments/*.md` — one file per detailed inline comment **Inline comment lines must be present in the PR diff.** GitHub review threads can only be attached to added or context lines inside a diff hunk. Now let me think about remaining deeper review aspects:

**A. Correctness of the new single-flight guard — one more edge case:**

```dart
Future<void> _persist() {
  final inFlight = _persistPass;
  if (inFlight != null) {
    _persistDirty = true;
    return inFlight;
  }
  return _persistPass = _persistLoop();
}
```

`_persistLoop` sets `_persistPass = null` in its `finally`. Consider: loop A running. Trigger B joins (dirty=true, awaits A). Loop A's current sweep finishes, dirty→true so re-sweeps. During re-sweep, trigger C joins (dirty=true, awaits A). Loop A re-sweeps again... converges when no more triggers land during sweeps. Fine.

Now the subtle one: **`_persistSoon` fire-and-forget with `.catchError` on a JOINED future.** `inFlight.catchError(...)` attaches to loop A's future. If loop A fails, both B's catchError and (for the finalizer) the try/catch handle it. But there's an asymmetry: when `_persistSoon` STARTS the loop (B is the starter), the loop future is wrapped: `unawaited(_persist().catchError(...))`. The un-wrapped loop future has ONE handler (the catchError's derived future is unawaited — but the ORIGINAL future's error flows into `.catchError`, which returns a NEW future whose error is swallowed... wait, does the original future count as "handled"? `.catchError` registers a handler on the original future — yes, handled.

When the finalizer STARTS the loop: `await _persist()` inside try/catch. Handled.

But here's an edge: the finalizer STARTS the loop and awaits it in try/catch; MEANWHILE a `_persistSoon` joins with `.catchError`. The loop SUCCEEDS. Fine.

Another edge: `_persistSoon` joins, attaching `.catchError`; the finalizer ALSO joined earlier via `await` in try/catch. Both handle. Fine.

What if `_persistSoon` starts the loop and its `catchError` swallows; then dispose() happens mid-loop? Loop continues, appends to session — session file ops on disposed service. `dispose` doesn't null `_session`. Pre-existing semantics (old code same). Not a regression.

**B. The dirty-flag re-run: `_persistedCount` last-writer-wins claim.**

`_persistUnchecked` sets `_persistedCount = all.length` at the end. Concurrent mutation of `_agent.state.messages` DURING the sweep: `for (final message in all.skip(_persistedCount))` — `all` is the LIVE list (`_agent.state.messages`). If a message is appended to the list WHILE the for-loop iterates it, the iterator sees it (live list) — that's fine, and `_persistedCount = all.length` at the end covers it. But could a message be REMOVED mid-sweep (reset/branch-switch)? `_persistedCount` bookkeeping vs. concurrent `reset()` — pre-existing hazard, unchanged by this PR.

Hmm — one NEW subtle issue though: the old chain guaranteed strict ordering: `_persistChain = _persistChain.then((_) => _persist())`. Each queued pass started only after the previous completed. The new single-flight loop merges passes but sweeps the same live state — equivalent or better. 

**C. `await inFlight` returns the LOOP's completion — including ALL coalesced re-sweeps.** The finalizer's comment claims "Awaiting this returns only when every pass queued so far has drained". TRUE: a trigger landing before the loop's final dirty-check causes another sweep; the await covers it.

BUT WAIT — one real gap: a trigger landing AFTER `_persistPass = null` (loop ended) starts a NEW loop. If the finalizer's `await _persist()` had joined the OLD loop, and a NEW pass starts after the old loop ended but before the finalizer's compaction... that's inherent to any concurrent system — the finalizer awaited only what was queued when IT called `_persist()`. Fine.

**D. Zone comment rationale** — "a chain head created at construction captures that zone" — `_persistChain = Future<void>.value()` was a field initializer, capturing the construction zone; chained `.then` listeners run in the head's zone. Under `tester.runAsync` (which runs in a different zone in fake_async widget tests), timers scheduled by the head zone never fire inside runAsync... plausible rationale for widget tests. The new approach stores `null` when idle, and `_persistLoop()`'s future is created in the CALLER's zone. OK — the comment is justified, and tests pass.

**E. Missing test for the coalescing path itself?** The new tests verify end state. There's no direct unit test asserting `_persistDirty` coalescing (that a trigger landing mid-sweep produces exactly ONE extra sweep). The second test's name says "coalesced persist passes land the full final state by idle" — it indirectly exercises the join path (finalizer joins in-flight pass from `_onMessageEnd`'s `_persistSoon`). Given the private fields, an additional test would need @visibleForTesting seams — not worth blocking. The end-state assertions are the right level.
